intro.label: What You'll Spend
intro.heading: Miniature American Shepherd First-Year Cost Breakdown
intro.html:
Miniature American Shepherds are small-to-medium dogs with moderate food costs and manageable grooming needs. Their primary health risks — Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA) and MDR1 drug sensitivity — both have DNA tests available, and responsible breeders test both parents for both conditions. Dog sport participation is a realistic ongoing cost for a breed that needs structured activity to thrive.

care.label: Biggest Costs
care.heading: Where MAS Ownership Gets Expensive
care.html:
CEA: Know the Status Before Purchase

Collie Eye Anomaly is present in the MAS breed. CEA ranges from mild choroidal hypoplasia (no vision impact) to severe coloboma or retinal detachment (significant vision loss). DNA testing identifies carriers and affected dogs — responsible breeders test both parents and do not produce affected puppies from known carriers. Ask for CEA test documentation before purchasing any puppy. An affected dog from untested parents carries a known, preventable condition.

MDR1 Drug Sensitivity

The MDR1 mutation affects many herding breeds including the MAS. An affected dog cannot safely receive ivermectin or certain other medications. DNA testing of both parents should be provided by responsible breeders. If documentation is not available, have your vet test the dog (~$80–$100). The result must be in the medical record and communicated at every medication decision.

Hip Dysplasia and Patellar Luxation

Both orthopedic conditions are documented in the breed. OFA hip and patellar clearances for both parents should be requested from the breeder. Surgical treatment for hip dysplasia costs $3,500–$7,000 per hip; patellar luxation surgery costs $1,500–$3,500 per knee. Pet insurance is the financial protection for these surgical risks.

special.label: Lifetime Budget
special.heading: Estimating Lifetime MAS Costs
special.html:
With a 12–13 year lifespan, Miniature American Shepherds have moderate annual costs. Their smaller size makes food costs lower than standard-sized herding breeds while their health risk profile is comparable.

ScenarioEstimated Lifetime Cost
Healthy dog, active sport life$18,000–$30,000
Patellar or orthopedic surgery required$24,000–$38,000
Multiple health interventions$32,000–$48,000+

MAS are a good value proposition for active owners — their smaller size reduces food costs compared to full-sized herding breeds while their sport and training capabilities are comparable. The health screening at purchase is the most important cost-control measure.

faq.q: What does a Miniature American Shepherd puppy cost from a reputable breeder?
faq.a: $800–$2,000 from breeders who test for CEA, MDR1, and provide OFA hip and patellar clearances for both parents. Both DNA tests are mandatory for responsible MAS breeding — a breeder who cannot provide these results is either not testing or testing and concealing results. The documentation is standard practice in responsible breeding programs.

faq.q: Do Miniature American Shepherds need a lot of exercise?
faq.a: Yes — they are a herding breed with significant energy and mental stimulation requirements. As adults, MAS need 60–90 minutes of activity daily, including mental engagement. Dog sports (agility, herding, disc) are popular with this breed. An under-exercised MAS will find other ways to use its energy, typically through destructive behavior. The breed's small size does not reduce its working drive.

faq.q: Is pet insurance worth it for a Miniature American Shepherd?
faq.a: Yes. The combination of hip dysplasia and patellar luxation risks means surgical orthopedic costs are a realistic possibility. Insurance enrolled before any conditions are documented covers hereditary conditions and provides protection against both major surgical events. The annual premium is modest relative to a single orthopedic surgery cost.
